question: My landlord wants me to leave after the first year, but I signed a five-year lease. Can they do that?
reference_answer: For a habitual-residence lease, if the agreed term is shorter than five years (or seven years when the landlord is a legal entity), it is generally extended annually until that minimum is reached, unless the tenant gives notice that they do not want to renew. There is a limited exception where an individual landlord needs the home for themselves or certain close family members, if the required need was expressly included in the contract and the legal conditions are met.

question: I want to move out before the end of my lease. How much notice do I have to give?
reference_answer: For a habitual-residence lease, the tenant can withdraw once at least six months have passed, by giving the landlord at least 30 days' notice. Under the current wording of this article, a withdrawal exercised this way does not give the landlord a right to compensation.

question: My landlord says I have to pay six months of rent upfront. Can they ask for that?
reference_answer: Unless the parties agree otherwise on the payment schedule, rent is paid monthly during the first seven days of the month. The landlord cannot require more than one month's rent to be paid in advance.

question: Can my landlord increase the rent every year if the contract does not say anything about updates?
reference_answer: No. The rent can only be updated annually if there is an express agreement allowing an update. If there is no express agreement, the rent is not updated.

question: My landlord says I have to pay for a broken boiler. Is that my responsibility?
reference_answer: The landlord must carry out repairs necessary to keep the home habitable, unless the damage is attributable to the tenant. The tenant is responsible for small repairs required by ordinary wear and tear.

question: How long does a stressed-rental-area declaration last, and can it be extended?
reference_answer: The declaration of a stressed residential-market area lasts three years. It can be extended year by year, following the same procedure, while the circumstances that justified it persist (and with the required justification).

question: My landlord wants to renovate the flat while I am living there. Do I have to let them?
reference_answer: The tenant must tolerate improvement works that cannot reasonably be postponed until the lease ends. The landlord must give written notice at least three months in advance, explaining the nature, start, duration and expected cost. The tenant may withdraw within one month of that notice unless the works have no effect or only an irrelevant effect on the home.

question: Can I remove a wall or make major changes to the apartment without asking the landlord?
reference_answer: No. The tenant needs the landlord's written consent for works that modify the home's configuration or its accessories. Works that reduce the home's stability or safety are never allowed.

question: My landlord is selling the apartment. Do I get the chance to buy it first?
reference_answer: As a general rule, the tenant has a right of first refusal (tanteo) when the rented home is sold, subject to the exceptions in the article. The landlord must notify the tenant of the decision to sell and the essential conditions; the tenant generally has 30 calendar days from the notification to exercise the right. The contract may include a valid waiver in the circumstances allowed by the article.

question: How much deposit can my landlord legally ask for when I rent a normal apartment?
reference_answer: The mandatory cash deposit (fianza) for a residential lease is one month's rent. The parties may agree on an additional guarantee, but for a habitual-residence lease of up to five years (or seven years if the landlord is a legal entity), that additional guarantee cannot exceed two months' rent.

question: When do I get my deposit back after handing over the keys?
reference_answer: The remaining deposit must be returned at the end of the lease. If it has not been returned within one month after the keys are handed over, the outstanding amount earns legal interest.

question: My landlord has not fixed a serious problem that makes the flat difficult to live in. What can I do?
reference_answer: The landlord is responsible for necessary repairs to keep the home habitable, unless the damage was caused by the tenant. The tenant should notify the landlord promptly. For qualifying habitability, safety or health defects, the tenant can make a written request with a reasonable estimate; the landlord has 15 calendar days to accept it, propose an alternative or carry out the repair. If there is no response or an unjustified refusal, the tenant may carry out the necessary repair and deduct its documented, reasonable cost from future rent.

question: Can my landlord charge me for the estate agent's fee for arranging the rental contract?
reference_answer: No. Property-management and contract-formalisation costs cannot be passed on to the tenant, directly or indirectly, under any name.

question: An owner in my building owes money to the community. Can they vote at the owners' meeting?
reference_answer: An owner who, when the meeting starts, is not up to date on all overdue community debts, and has not challenged them in court or deposited the amount in court or with a notary, may take part in the discussion but has no vote. The minutes record these owners, and their participation quota does not count towards the required majorities.

question: If I have to leave the apartment because of a fire that was not my fault, does the lease automatically continue?
reference_answer: The lease ends (it does not simply continue) if the rented property is lost for a cause not attributable to the landlord, or on a final declaration of ruin by the competent authority (Article 28). If the home is only made uninhabitable by conservation works or works ordered by an authority, Article 26 lets the tenant suspend the contract (the term and the rent are paused until the works end) or withdraw, without compensation.

question: Can I sublet my room to someone else while I am away for a few months?
reference_answer: A rented home may only be sublet partially and with the landlord's prior written consent. The sublet price cannot exceed the rent corresponding to the part being sublet, and the subtenant's right ends when the main tenant's lease ends.

question: My landlord has not given me a written receipt for rent. Are they supposed to?
reference_answer: Yes. The landlord must provide a receipt unless the parties use another payment method that proves the tenant has paid. The receipt or substitute document must separately identify the amounts paid, including the current rent.

question: The tenant who signed the lease has died. Can their partner or family member stay in the apartment?
reference_answer: Certain relatives and people who lived with the tenant may have a right to take over (subrogate into) the lease, if they meet the article's conditions and priority rules. The landlord must receive written notice of the death, the identity and relationship of the person taking over, and the required supporting evidence within three months of the tenant's death; otherwise the lease ends.

question: Before I sign a rental contract, what information can I ask the landlord to give me?
reference_answer: Before signing and before paying any amount on account, a person interested in renting a home can ask for, in accessible and durable form: the identity of the landlord (and any intermediary); the financial terms (total price and what it includes); the essential features of the home and building (habitability certificate, useful and built area, age of the building and main works, services and installations, energy-efficiency certificate, accessibility, occupancy status); and legal information on the property (land-registry identification, charges and the participation quota), plus other items such as protected-housing status.

question: My landlord says I have to pay the building's general expenses even though they are not written in my contract. Do I?
reference_answer: The tenant can only be made responsible for general building expenses if the parties agreed to it in writing and the contract states the annual amount of those expenses at the date of signing. Individual services measured by meters are paid by the tenant.

question: The apartment is in a declared stressed rental area and the owner is a large landlord. How is the rent for a new contract worked out?
reference_answer: In a declared stressed area, the rent for a new habitual-residence contract is generally limited by the previous rent for that home, updated under the previous contract's clause. Where the landlord is a large holder, the applicable reference-price index ceiling also applies. The Housing Act defines a large holder generally as someone owning more than ten urban residential properties or more than 1,500 m² of residential built area (excluding garages and storage rooms); in a stressed area, the regional declaration may lower the threshold to five or more residential properties in that area if justified.

question: My landlord owns several apartments and says they are not a large landlord. What does the law actually count?
reference_answer: The general definition is a person or company owning more than ten urban residential properties or more than 1,500 m² of residential built area, excluding garages and storage rooms. In a stressed area, the regional declaration may specify a lower threshold of five or more residential properties in that area. The LAU uses this definition when applying the rent ceiling for certain new contracts in stressed areas.

question: My lease is ending in a stressed area. Can I ask to stay for another year or two?
reference_answer: If the home is in a declared stressed area and the declaration is still in force when the relevant mandatory or tacit extension ends, the tenant can request extraordinary annual extensions for up to three years. The landlord must generally accept, subject to the exceptions in Article 10.3, such as an agreed alternative, a new contract within the applicable rent limits, or a qualifying need for the landlord to occupy the home.

question: My landlord wants me to pay community fees. Who is actually responsible for those costs under the rental and community laws?
reference_answer: Under the LAU, the tenant can be made to pay general community expenses only if the lease contains a written agreement specifying their annual amount. Under the Horizontal Property Act, the owner is the person legally obliged to contribute to the community's general expenses according to their participation quota. So the community's claim is against the owner; the lease may separately allow the owner to pass qualifying expenses on to the tenant.

question: The building approves a major repair and sends everyone a special assessment. Can the landlord make me pay it?
reference_answer: The LPH places the obligation to contribute to general community expenses and building costs on the owner, according to the participation quota. The LAU only allows general expenses to be passed to the tenant through a written agreement that specifies the annual amount at the date of the contract. The tenant is responsible for small repairs caused by ordinary wear and tear, not automatically for the owner's community assessment or major building works.

question: I rent a flat in a building where the owners vote to ban tourist rentals. Does that decision apply to my landlord?
reference_answer: The LPH allows the owners' meeting to approve, limit, condition or prohibit tourist-rental activity with the support of three-fifths of all owners who also represent three-fifths of the participation quotas. It can also approve special expense quotas or increase the common-expense share for the affected home by up to 20%. These agreements are not retroactive. The LPH links this activity to the tourist-rental category referred to in Article 5.e of the LAU.

question: My landlord says they can raise the rent because they renovated the apartment. Can they do that, and how do the community rules affect it?
reference_answer: Under the LAU, after five years of the lease (or seven years if the landlord is a legal entity), the landlord may generally increase rent for qualifying improvement works, unless the contract says otherwise. The increase is calculated using the legally specified formula and cannot exceed 20% of the rent then in force; public subsidies are deducted from the investment. Separately, the LPH makes the owner responsible for community expenses according to their quota, so ordinary community charges are not automatically the tenant's responsibility.

question: The landlord sold the apartment while I was still renting it. Does the buyer have to respect my lease, and who pays the community debt?
reference_answer: Under the LAU, the buyer is generally subrogated into the landlord's position for the legally protected minimum period, subject to the article's conditions and the relevant registration rules. Under the LPH, the buyer is also liable with the acquired property for community debts attributable to the previous owners for the current year and the three preceding calendar years. These are separate rules: one protects the tenancy, the other secures the community's debt.
